title: The Dharma of Zen Poetry
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads "The Dharma of Zen Poetry," a talk by Deirdre Asho Peterson of Red Rocks Zen Circle in Sedona, which Nomon found while preparing retreat talks on the poet Ryokan. Peterson finds the three marks of existence running through poems by Han Shan, Ryokan, Isa, Li Po, Ikkyu and Basho. Isa's poem on his daughter's death ends with "This world is a dewdrop world. And yet." Nomon adds asides on Ryokan playing with children using string balls, and on Han Shan's invitation to "leap the world's ties." Peterson closes by urging Zen students not to put practice off.

It's your house.
So that's what she does.
That's very common.

You hear about the ones that have organizational structure, but a lot more of them are like her place, Red Rocks Zen Circle.

It's called The Dharma of Zen Poetry.
I'm reading her:

*We often have a text or a sutra as a focus for the study period, but recently we were studying something a little differently, which is the poetry of Zen, and it's been a real pleasure to read these beautiful poems in haiku, and I wanted to tell you a little more about these poems and explore what they offer for our practice.
What makes a poem a Zen poem?
In many cases, the poems were written by Zen monks, but there are other beautiful Zen poems written by those who studied and practiced the way as lay people, too.
To me, the Zen flavor of these poems comes not from whether the writer was wearing a monastic robe, but from how their writings convey the essence of Zen in a poetic form.
These poems show the realization of their writers in the profound truth expressed in simple and direct language.*
*The Zen poets we usually talk about lived in China and later in Japan.
The span of time involved is a long one.
For example, Han Shan, also known as Cold Mountain,* that's what that means, *is one of the best known Zen poets.
The dates of his life are hazy, but scholars generally place him in China in the 8th century, so about the time of the early Middle Ages in Europe.
Towards the end of this period, almost 1,000 years later, is the beloved Japanese poet Ryokan.* That's how I found this.
*He was writing his verses about 200 years ago.*
*A good number of these Zen poets lived solitary lives as hermits or as wanderers.
They left their monastic communities to live what they felt was a more authentic Zen life, with fewer comforts usually and fewer people, a simpler life with a closeness to nature.
To see this intimacy, to live this intimacy with the natural world, and it's in their writing, a lived-in familiarity with birds and grasses, the cold of winter, the starkness of the high mountains.
The poem suggests that all we need to know of the Dharma is revealed in nature, if we have eyes to see.
Here is the poet Ikkyu writing in 15th century Japan.*
This is a famous Ikkyu poem.
*Every day priests examine the Dharma and endlessly chant complicated sutras.
Before doing that, they should learn how to read the love letters sent by wind and rain, snow and moon.
Every day priests examine the Dharma and endlessly chant complicated sutras.
Before doing that, they should learn how to read the love letters sent by the wind and rain, snow and moon.*
*What struck me in reading these Zen poems was how much they're filled with what are known as the three marks of existence.* It's a great insight, I think.
*The three marks, or the three truths, are a kind of foundational underpinning for all Buddhist teachings.
They are impermanence, suffering, and what is called non-self, or not-self.
In other words, that life has suffering and dissatisfaction, the things that come into existence pass out of existence, and that there's no separate, unchanging self amidst the sea of change.
And while we can talk about these three truths separately, so impermanence, suffering, not-self, they're actually tightly interwoven, just different aspects of the same thing.

For example, in Zen poems, the awareness of impermanence is often closely interwoven with the suffering that this impermanence can bring, the sadness or poignancy or loneliness we experience in a world that is passing.
Ryokan wrote,*
*No bird above these wild hills.
Garden leaves fall one by one.
Desolate autumn winds.
A man alone in thin black robes.
No bird above these wild hills.
Garden leaves fall one by one.
Desolate autumn winds.
A man alone in thin black robes.*

*And the poets have a keen sense of the passage of time and sickness and old age and death that's part of our conditioned existence, and it gives the world its shimmering beauty as well as its sorrow.* I agree with you there.
The poems can really express that, right?
The beauty and the sorrow.
*Han Shan wrote, The peach blossoms would like to stay through the summer but the winds and moon carry them on and will not wait.
The peach blossoms would like to stay through the summer but the winds and moons carry them on and will not wait.
And the Japanese poet Isa writes this haiku, All around my house pond frogs from the beginning sang about old age.* Old frogs.
*All around my house pond frogs from the beginning sang about old age.*
*But what we find in these poems is not denial.
Not denial of the pain or the loss.
Nor do we find a cold, austere detachment either.
Instead we find a perspective that is very real and very human.
And as Zen practitioners we may have a deep sense of impermanence but as humans we grieve deeply.
The Japanese poet Isa, known for his haiku in journals, writes very poignantly about this in his narrative called The Spring of My Life.* I guess he wrote a kind of biography, I never knew that.
*Isa was a man intimately acquainted with pain and loss.
He watched all of his three children and then his wife die of various causes.
He writes about the death of his daughter.*
*How can I, her father, stand by and watch her fade away each day like a perfect flower ravaged by rain and mud?
How can I, her father, stand by and watch her fade away each day like a perfect flower ravaged by rain and mud?
And then he wrote, finally at midsummer as the morning glory flowers were closing, her eyes closed forever.
I saw her mother's heartbreak but knew that tears were useless, that water under the bridge never returns, that scattered flowers are gone forever.
Yet nothing I could do would cut the bonds of human love.*
And then this is his super famous poem, Isa.
I have a nice calligraphy of this.
*This world is a dewdrop world.
And yet.*
Yeah, I know that "and yet" just makes you shiver, doesn't it?
**Participant:** My husband's headstone has been installed today.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Oh, is that right, Catherine?
No, no, don't be, don't be.
Oh, that's beautiful, yeah.
Wow.
*This world is a dewdrop world and yet.* Beautiful, "and yet," yeah.
Beautiful man, and yet, right.
*Poets also find their way to express the mystery that is the heart of the third truth of existence, and that is of our not-self, our changing, that there is no separate unchanging self.
This sense of no fixed self is conveyed through the poet's direct simple language in which there appears to be no ego operating but just direct experience.* Direct experience as not-self, right?
Losing yourself in nature.
*Here's a well-known verse written by Li Po, a Chinese poet from about the same time as Han Shan.*
*We sit together, the mountain and me, until only the mountain remains.
We sit together, the mountain and me, until only the mountain remains.*
We all know that feeling, right?
And then you're checking your phone or whatever, there's those moments, right?
Oh, it's just the mountain.
Are we the mountain?
Is the mountain us?
Hard to say.
*And Ryokan wrote, the winds have died, flowers go on falling, birds call, silence penetrates each song.
The mystery, unknowable, unlearnable.
The winds have died, flowers go on falling, birds call, silence penetrates each song.
The mystery, unknowable, unlearnable.*
*So we can really see how the Zen poems are flavored by deep intimacy with the three truths.
Another defining element of this poetry is that it conveys a sense of depth, of deep stillness that is there in the midst of change.
Stillness in change.
We could experience it ourselves as a silent presence that underlies the arising and passing away of phenomena.
The Japanese poet Basho writes this, lonely stillness, a single cicada's cry, sinking into stone.* You feel the way that just kind of, *a lonely stillness, a single cicada's cry, sinking into stone.*
*We can see from these writings that these poets cultivated a deeper inner stillness.
They live their daily life, they live their practice, listening deeply in touch with inner and outer stillness.

And while it seems that most of the Zen writings express the poet's experience of the natural world, sometimes the poets also speak to us directly, as our teachers, encouraging us to get to what is important.
In his usual unpretentious style, Ryokan wrote,*
*My hut lies in the middle of dense forest.
Each year the green ivy grows longer.
No news of the affairs of people.
On the occasional song of a woodcutter, I have nothing to report my friends.
If you want to find the meaning, stop chasing after so many things.
My hut lies in the middle of dense forest.
Each year the green ivy grows longer and longer.
No news comes of the affairs of people.
On the occasional song of a woodcutter, I have nothing to report my friends.
If you want to find the meaning, stop chasing after so many things.*

We know he went to town every couple of days.
He also liked to drink and hang out.

One of the things he always had in the sleeves of his robes, which have a kind of pocket in here, was some balls made out of string that he made, so he could throw them for the kids.
So he wasn't just peacefully, although he did sit a lot, and it sounded like he sat a lot at night.
He writes about sitting at night and studying at night.
Anyway, here's Han Shan.

And not much to look at.

So Cold Mountain is both the place and the name that he took.
He has a cave on Cold Mountain.
You may think I'm crazy, but come on up.
Make it to Cold Mountain.
He also writes,
*Cold Mountain is a house without beams or walls.
The six doors left and right are open.
At the center, nothing.
Cold Mountain is a house without beams or walls.
The six doors left and right are open.
At the center, nothing.*
So the six doors, you know, are the six senses.
Everything's open and the self is empty.
At the center, nothing.

He writes further, I climb to Cold Mountain, the road to Cold Mountain that never ends.
Who can leap the world's ties and sit with me among the clouds?
I climb the road to Cold Mountain, the road to Cold Mountain that never ends.
Who can leap the world's ties and sit with me among white clouds?*
Doesn't that make you want to go?
Me, me, can I go?
May I sit with you?
Let go of the world's ties.
I thought of a new technology.

Wouldn't that be good?
I can move to Silicon Valley and patent that.
Get angel investors and get rich.
See, huh?
Free people, it's liberative.
Anyway, that's what Cold Mountain was saying though, right?
Leap the world's ties, delete your calendar.
And here's her conclusion.
*There are a good number of people who are not involved with formal Zen practice, but who also enjoy reading these haiku and Zen verses.
I know that I like to read them long before I started practice.
But all of us here in the Zendo are here because we're looking to live and experience the teachings, not just because we like poetry.
So as Zen practitioners, the poems speak to us in a different way.
They remind us that time passes swiftly.
And we should not put off practice until some vague time in the future, when it will be more convenient.
The poems inspire us to connect with the natural world also, because nature can be a portal out of the world of thinking and doing and into the world of being.
The poems remind us a way of experiencing the world and being in the world that is easy to lose sight of.
They encourage us to slow down and be present to ourselves and the world around us.
These poems are messengers.
And I encourage you to see what the message these poems speak to you.*
Isn't that a nice talk?
I'm so impressed.
So, Deirdre Asho Peterson.
I think she studied in a Zen center in New York or something like that.
Red Rocks Zen Circle.
And by the way, I'm reasonably good at getting notes to Michael to put on the website, which is a really good one for me, remembering a link to it and everything.
You can read it again.
And some nice tips on good Zen poets in there, too.
I mean, that's good for tonight, huh?
Thanks for coming.
The Zendo keeps going.
Lots of people, a couple of people.
I guess it would still be here if there was nobody here.
